newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy says Castro is "open to dialogue" on reforms.
newsitem.headline: Italy says Castro is "open to dialogue" on reforms.

text.p: Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini said on Monday he discussed democratic reforms with Cuban President Fidel Castro and found him "open to dialogue".

Castro, who attended a U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit last week and will hold an historic audience with Pope John Paul on Tuesday, held court in his Rome hotel as a string of visitors arrived for talks or to pay homage to an icon of communism.

Dini told reporters after nearly an hour of talks that he and Castro discussed the prospect of boosting cooperation between the European Union and Cuba. He said Castro, 70, spoke of economic development and human rights "without difficulty".
"He presented the present system that he defends, concerning the rights of citizens of Cuba, including the present electoral system," Dini said. "I found him open to dialogue."
Castro appeared on Sunday to rule out any change to the course he has steered his country along since 1959, despite the fall of the Berlin Wall and collapse of communism elsewhere.
"We have achieved things which I do think deserve respect...We are achieving miracles," he told a news conference.
"How have we done this? Thanks to the revolution, because the revolution opened the door -- with no need for any other opening, which would be called counter-revolution," he said.
Cuban exiles used Castro's rare visit to Europe to protest at alleged human rights abuses. Castro retorted by extolling the virtues of Cuba's healthcare and low infant mortality rate.
Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar has led calls within the 15-nation EU for greater democracy in the Caribbean island, saying Cuba must make the first move to boost ties with Europe.
Cuba needs European links since the United States imposed a trade embargo 34 years ago to try to flush Castro from power.

The European Union is in favour of lifting the blockade, and opposes a hardening in Washington's stance with the Helms-Burton law allowing Cuban-Americans to sue foreign firms or individuals who own or operate properties seized by Castro's government.

"We discussed the prospect of going ahead with preparations in the course of 1997 for a cooperation and commercial agreement with the European Union," Dini said. Talks on reaching an accord began earlier this year but have become stalled.
"It seems to me there are openings for continuing dialogue," Dini said. "There is nothing to lose from dialogue. I think we all have to gain, both the Europeans and the Americans."
Castro's visit has caused a sensation in Italy, which once boasted the biggest Marxist party in the West and now has a centre-left government dominated by ex-communists.
Opposition politicians say they are disgusted at the red-carpet treatment reserved for Castro, who has been flanked by heavily armed police and whisked through Rome like royalty.
Leading Italian leftists filed in before Dini to pay tribute to the "lider maximo" (great leader), who stole the show at the five-day food summit, signing autographs on request.

"He's not a man with an extraordinary past, but a man of the present," said Fausto Bertinotti, whose hardline Communist Refoundation party is a key political ally of the government. "He's maybe the last great political leader on a world scale."

But Massimo D'Alema, leader of the ex-communist Democratic Party of the Left, the main party in government, said he had discussed political "renewal" with Castro. "Naturally we spoke of...democratic reforms which we judge necessary," he added.
